::: {#about .page-section}
## About

::: {.about-text}
I study how action, perception, and brain development are connected in infancy and childhood. With students and collaborators, I use EEG to look at how infants and children respond to touch, to watching other people act, and to events they are expecting. Recent work asks how infants' reaching and grasping relate to body maps in the infant brain, using computer vision to measure hand movements. I also work with colleagues on children's interactions with social robots and with AI-generated content.

I have also written a series of theory papers on embodiment, development, and how psychology and neuroscience relate to each other. A recurring question in that work is what the organization and activity of living things can tell us about cognition and experience.

My undergraduate degree was in Natural Sciences at the University of Cambridge, where I specialized in zoology. I stayed on at Cambridge for a Ph.D. in developmental psychology that drew on the ethological tradition. Under Joan Stevenson-Hinde's supervision, my dissertation examined the continuity of behavioral inhibition from 4 to 7 years of age and its relations to psychophysiological measures.

In 1997 I joined Nathan Fox's lab in the Department of Human Development at the University of Maryland, first as a postdoctoral researcher and later as a Research Assistant Professor. I worked on temperament, attachment, early experience, and brain development, and learned to record EEG in infants and young children. Toward the end of that time I became interested in the sensorimotor mu rhythm, which turned my attention to perception and action. I followed that line when I moved to Temple in 2004. With Andrew Meltzoff and other colleagues, I studied how carrying out an action changes the brain's response to watching someone else do something similar, and went on to study self–other correspondence and body maps in infancy. Over the same period, conversations at Temple, especially with Willis Overton, drew me toward theories of embodiment and relational developmental systems.

I have an article forthcoming in a special issue of *Perspectives on Psychological Science* that brings together some of my writing on embodiment to outline how psychology might become a "developmental science of living sense-making" over the next century. For links to the article itself and a deeper dive into the background and context, I wrote this [précis and author commentary](/psychology-2125.html).

From 2016 to 2026 I served as Chair of the Department of Psychology and Neuroscience at Temple. I have also served as President of the Society for the Study of Human Development.

::: {#resources .page-section}
## Open Resources

::: {.section-intro}
I have put together two freely available online resources that grew out of my teaching and writing on development and embodiment.
:::

::: {.project-list}
::: {.project-item}
### [About Development](https://aboutdevelopment.org/)

About Development is a set of readings on what development is and how it works. The central question is why development reliably occurs when there is no plan for the finished organism present at earlier stages. It introduces a broad approach to thinking about development that is meant to be of interest to anyone who wants to go beyond the description of "what happens and when" in development.
:::

::: {.project-item}
### [Enacting Life](https://enacting.life/)

Enacting Life is a companion set of readings introducing enactivism, a way of thinking about cognition that begins with the organization and activity of living things. The readings follow the biological strand of this approach, rooted in the work of the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, and consider how it might help ground psychology and neuroscience more coherently in biology. A key theme is what makes living things different from nonliving things, particularly machines. The resource ends with a coda on AI and its place in human sense-making.
:::
